lines.text: of the spirit have heard the voice of God; men for whom there
was no doubt that only faithful devotion to the invisible
world of the spirit could endow life with dignity and nobility;
men who bore within themselves the consciousness of an
inner peace of which neither the fierce hostility of nature nor
the wickedness of man could rob them. And there were also
men who spoke of these things in paradoxes similar to those
of Paul. The description of the true sage as the Stoic Epictetus
describes it can be an admonishment and summons even to
the Christian:
"In sickness and yet blessed,
In dangers and yet blessed,
In death and yet blessed,
In exile and yet blessed,
In disgrace and yet blessed."
II
This description of the true sage is of course not yet the
description of the true Christian as the words of Paul picture
it for us. Yet there exists between the two ideals a character-
istic affinity; it is the affinity between idealism and Christian-
ity. A dangerous affinity, we may and indeed must say!
For it has often led to a confusion between Christianity and
idealism, and for this reason, especially in recent times, it
has caused the Church to attack idealism. But to-day above
all it would be disastrous, just because of this danger, to fail
to recognize this inner kinship. Let us consider. Was it not
one and the selfsame time in which Nietzsche's cry rang out:
"God is dead!" and in which faith in the world of the spirit
died in our culture? The gospel addresses itself to man; but
what alone makes man truly human is his participation in the
world of the spirit. And as, in the Pauline phrase, the Mosaic
law was formerly a "custodian until Christ came"
, so also 1s
idealism. Naturally, as the Judaic law was misused by man
to enable him to establish his own righteousness in the sight of
God, the same possibility of abuse exists with regard to idealism.
